headline: Midnight Outgoing: Bass in the Inlet Hole, Weakfish Still Chewing at the Bridge
subhead: With the moon filling toward August and the bay running warm, the smart money's after dark — here's where I'm putting my time this week.
body_markdown:
I turned down an easy afternoon fluke charter this week to sit on the jetty rocks at 1 a.m. instead, and I don't regret it. That's the decision every Shinnecock angler needs to make right now — day or night — and with the bay running warm and slick on top, night is where the fish actually are.

Here's my thinking. The surface water out front is sitting in the low 70s, same story from the Bight buoy off the beach to the flats inside the bay, and that kind of warmth pushes striped bass off the daytime bite almost entirely. They're not gone — they're just smart. During daylight they're holding deep against structure, tucked into the current seams off the north jetty and the deeper cuts by the Coast Guard station, riding the thermocline where it exists. Come dark, with the water cooling a couple degrees and bait starting to move, they slide up onto the rocks and into the inlet throat to feed. That's the window I fish, and it's been worth the lost sleep.

My pattern this week has been simple: get to the inlet an hour before the tide turns, fish the last of the incoming quiet, then really go to work once the outgoing gets some shoulder to it — usually two to three hours into the ebb. That's when bait gets pulled out of the bay and pinned against the rocks and the pilings, and the bass stack up in the deep hole on the ocean side of the East Jetty, 15 to 20 feet, current ripping. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig have been steady, but the better fish — a few pushing 30-plus inches — have come on live eels drifted right along the rock face, letting the current do the work instead of retrieving them like a lure. Slow presentation, heavy leader, because those rocks will cut you off if you get lazy.

Ponquogue Bridge is still doing its thing, and this is where I'd send anybody who doesn't want to fight inlet current at 2 a.m. Weakfish are holding tight to the pilings on the bay side, and the bite's been best on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current slackens enough to work a bucktail without getting swept sideways. Half-ounce chartreuse bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or a live spearing have been the ticket, worked slow along the base of the pilings in 12 to 18 feet. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts mixed with a few keeper-class fish in the 16 to 18-inch range — so it's not a slam dunk, but it's been consistent enough that I've made the drive out more nights than not.

Fluke has softened up in the open flats the way it does every summer once the shallow bay water gets uncomfortably warm — that pattern's holding true again this year. The fish that are still biting well have pushed into the deeper channel bends and the inlet-adjacent structure, which tracks with what's happening from Barnegat on up. My best drifts lately have been along the edge of the main channel just inside the inlet and down toward the canal mouth, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, staying tight to the bottom on the tail end of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Nothing giant, but a few 4 and 5-pound fish have come out of there, and that's a lot better than the dink-only reports I'm hearing from guys still drifting the open flats near Tiana.

Bluefish are around but you have to catch them at the right moment — bunker schools have been running the ocean side of the inlet and occasionally pushing bait right up against the jetty rocks on the tail of the incoming, which turns into a short, violent window if you're there for it. Poppers and metal on wire leader, cast right at the boil. It doesn't last, so don't wander far if you see the birds working.

Porgies are still a reliable bay bet if you want a box of fish for the table without the drama — sandworms and squid strips on high tide around Tiana Beach in 8 to 12 feet, simple high-low rigs, nothing fancy needed. Blackfish are still a ways off; water's too warm yet, that'll be a fall conversation.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August and that's going to put more push into every tide stage — good news for current-dependent spots like the inlet hole and the canal mouth, where stronger water usually means a sharper bite window rather than a longer one. I'd also keep half an eye on the inlet itself over the next couple weeks — this is exactly the kind of water that tips over into false albacore territory once temps cross the right threshold, and Shinnecock's been a launching point for that before. Nothing confirmed yet, but if bait starts getting nervous out front, that's your sign. For now, if you've only got one night this week, I'd take the outgoing after midnight at the inlet and work the eel along the rocks. It's not a guaranteed fish, but it's where the biggest ones have been showing up.
